subject: Agriculture
title: Mad Cow Disease
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Mad Cow Disease.

hook.text: In the 1990s, British beef gave people a fatal brain disease. The cause was horrifying: feeding cows to cows.

buildup.text: To boost protein cheaply, meat-and-bone meal from slaughtered cattle was mixed into cattle feed.

discovery.text: A misfolded protein—a prion—spread through this cannibalistic cycle, causing BSE in cattle and CJD in humans.

twist.text: Prions can't be killed by cooking, bleach, or radiation. They're nearly indestructible infectious agents.

climax.text: The crisis collapsed the British beef market and led to the slaughter of 4.4 million cattle.

punchline.text: We turned herbivores into cannibals. Nature punished the shortcut.

quiz.question: What caused mad cow disease (BSE)?
options: Prions spread by feeding meat-and-bone meal from cattle to cattle

details.summary: Mad cow disease (BSE) is a fatal brain disease in cattle caused by misfolded proteins called prions, transmitted through contaminated feed made from rendered animal parts. This topic covers the 1990s UK epidemic, its link to human vCJD, and the reforms it triggered.
details.whyItMatters: The BSE crisis killed 178 people, destroyed billions in cattle industry value, and fundamentally changed how the world regulates animal feed and food safety.
takeaways: BSE spread through cattle feed containing rendered brain and spinal cord from infected animals
Over 4.4 million UK cattle were slaughtered to control the epidemic in the 1990s
BSE led to variant CJD in humans—a fatal brain disease with no cure

faq.question: What caused the mad cow disease epidemic?
faq.answer: BSE spread because cattle were fed protein supplements made from rendered remains of other cattle, including brain and spinal tissue. The infective agent—a misfolded prion protein—survived the rendering process and accumulated in the food chain.

faq.question: How did mad cow disease change food safety regulations?
faq.answer: Most countries banned feeding animal protein to ruminants, introduced mandatory BSE testing, required removal of specified risk materials at slaughter, established traceability systems, and created new food safety agencies with greater regulatory power.
